title: The women in the garden
hookLine: the women are sent to charm him, and he stays unmoved (Buddhacarita 4)

lines: A GARDEN, MUSIC, THE COURT'S WOMEN.
cards: The king has heard. His son came home from the road shaken, and now he won't stop thinking about old age and death. So the king reaches for the tool he trusts.

He sends the prince to a beautiful garden outside the city, and sends the women of the court with him. Their task is plain: delight him, bring him back to the life of pleasure, make him forget what he saw.
Music under the trees. Flowers. Laughter by the water.
The poem lingers in this garden, and every line is built to pull a young man's attention away from one thought.

teach.b: First, the women. They didn't choose this. They were sent, by a king, with a task.
At first, the poem says, they hold back, shy before the prince.

Then they're urged on, and they do what they were told: they sing and dance, tease and whisper, wander close in the flowering garden, described with all the color and play of court poetry. Second, the prince.
He doesn't scold them or run. He simply isn't moved.

teach.h: HE SEES WHAT THE ROAD TAUGHT HIM.
teach.b: He looks at the young women, bright and laughing, and sees what the road just taught him: this beauty will age, these bodies will sicken, these lives will end.
He's not cold toward them. He's thinking about them more truly than the garden wants him to. Third, steadiness.
Unmoved doesn't mean frozen, or proud, or disgusted.
In the Anguttara Nikaya the Buddha names eight worldly conditions, gain and loss, good name and bad name, praise and blame, pleasure and pain, and describes a mind they don't overturn.
In the garden only the pleasant half is pulling, and steadiness looks like quiet. And fourth, the cost to the king.
Another remedy has failed, and the poem blames no one in the garden.
The women did what they were asked. The prince did what he couldn't help. And before he goes home, a friend will try.

how: Some Buddhist teachers use the garden scene when speaking about sense pleasures and restraint, and in temple murals the prince is sometimes shown seated calmly among dancers and musicians.

o: proud contempt for the pleasures of others
a mind the world's ups and downs don't tip over
a cold refusal to feel anything at all

p: sends the women to delight him
beauty that will age and end

s: in the poem, the women set out to trap the prince on their own
the king sends them with a task.
the prince scolds the women and leaves
he stays, courteous and unmoved, thinking of age and death.
the garden blooms and the music plays, and the prince comes home with the same thought.

games.q: you're the prince, in a flowering garden, surrounded by music and laughter meant to make you forget the road. what do you do?
o: give in and forget what you saw.
stay where you are, courteous, and keep seeing clearly.
shout at everyone and storm home.
games.why: he stays unmoved. not cold, not angry: he sees the beauty and also where it ends.

practice: Picture one thing that pulls at you on an ordinary day, the phone face-down on the table, a snack you're not hungry for, a show that starts the next episode on its own, and feel the pull honestly.
Then breathe, and let it rise and pass without obeying it. You're not fighting it; you're just not moved.

wordCard.voice: steadiness. What the prince shows when the court women are sent to charm him in the garden: courteous, unmoved, already thinking of age and death beneath the beauty. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: unmoved. Courteous and kind, and still not carried off by the garden. See you tomorrow.
